title: Model selection playbook walkthrough — Veridian Financial
summary: AE + SE walked through Redwood's model catalog playbook focused on picking open models for a production fraud-detection assistant. Reviewed benchmark interpretation, compatibility matrix, and pilot options (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Customer requested a short hosted benchmark, security pack, and a follow-up SE-led deep dive about private deployment networking.
topics: benchmark score interpretation (latency, p95, token cost)
compatibility matrix: quantization and kernel mapping
deployment tradeoffs: hosted vs dedicated vs private
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-27 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Samir, Laura, Ben, Nina (Veridian)
Links shared: demo deck https://redwood-demo.s3/model-playbook.pdf, bench sheet https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/benchmark-vid

Summary (auto): quick playbook, prioritized shortlist, bench request, security pack to follow

[00:00] Maya: All right good afternoon everyone thanks for carving time. I'm Maya with Redwood, this is Ethan our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Ben: Good, thanks. Busy but excited to see this.
[00:14] Samir: Yeah appreciate it, we'll probably be a little bit detail-y on infra and perf.
[00:20] Ethan: Perfect that's what I want to hear. We'll focus the first 20 on the catalog flow and then go deeper on compatibility and benching.
[00:30] Laura: Great. Quick note, timeline is quarter end for a pilot approval so around mid-September would be ideal.
[00:38] Maya: Good to know, we'll try to surface a clear pilot plan today.
[00:42] Ethan: Okay jumping in, here's the playbook slide — step one is shortlist by capability and cost. We show curated open models, performance profiles, and a compatibility matrix that maps models to runtime kernels and quant profiles.
[01:05] Samir: When you say "compat matrix" is that per-GPU or per-kernel?
[01:09] Ethan: Good question. It's both. We have a model x hardware matrix and then a kernel/quantization readiness row. So you'd see, for ex, Llama-2-13B quantized to 4-bit with A100 kernels gives you X latency, while the same quant profile on V100 shows different perf.
[01:28] Nina: Is that data from your public benchmarks or from customer runs?
[01:32] Ethan: Mostly Redwood lab benches standardized across our infra, but we attach a confidence band and we recommend a short customer run to validate prompts — prompt distribution matters a lot.
[01:43] Ben: Right that's the key for us — our prompt lengths spike occasionally, especially with multi-turn sessions. p95 tail matters more than mean.
[01:52] Ethan: Totally, we highlight p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens. Also we surface typical KV cache hit rate impact — sorry sometimes transcripts write that as K V cash —
[02:05] Samir: (laughs) we've seen that. Do you support prefix/KV caching across model variants?
[02:10] Ethan: Yes. The runtime has KV cache semantics and we can persist warm prefixes for the session layer with TTL. It reduces effective per-token compute for long context reuse.
[02:21] Laura: Can you show an example of the compatibility matrix?
[02:24] Ethan: Sure, switching to the console: filter by objective = retrieval augmented generation, latency SLO = 200ms. The catalog highlights three open models: oxford-13b-lite, river-7b-instruct, and harbor-13b-quant. Each has a recommended kernel and quantization profile.
[02:40] Maya: I'll call out the playbook — start with a 3-model shortlist, run a prompt set bench, then pick a champion and do a canary on dedicated or private depending on data constraints.
[02:52] Samir: How often do you see the catalog recommendations change? Like when new kernels drop or new quant techniques appear?
[02:58] Ethan: We refresh the catalog weekly for patch-level kernel updates and monthly for model revisions. For big changes (eg a new quant method), we surface as a migration note and include a regression eval.
[03:12] Ben: On data sensitivity — we will likely need private deployment for PCI-adjacent data. What's the gap between hosted and private?
[03:20] Maya: Hosted is fastest to get started; private gives you VPC-onboarding, KMS/HSM keys, and audit logs. Dedicated is the middle ground — reserved GPU pools with tenant isolation but control plane still managed by Redwood.
[03:34] Samir: For private, networking is a blocker. Do you support customer-managed gateways and on-prem GPU hosts?
[03:41] Ethan: Yes, we support VPC peering, private endpoints, and an on-prem package. For on-prem, we provide an orchestrator agent that maps to your cluster; networking depends on your team's firewall rules but we've done similar setups with bank customers.
[03:56] Nina: Ok cool. Back to the bench numbers, can you show the bench sheet for harbor-13b-quant?
[04:01] Ethan: Pulling it up — here's p50 80ms p95 310ms on A100-80GB with the quant profile, cost estimate 0.12 per 1k tokens. Note the p95 is higher because the model uses long context and attention kernels spike for certain sequences.
[04:20] Laura: That p95 is above our 250ms SLO. How do we reduce it?
[04:24] Ethan: Two levers: change model/quant profile (pick a smaller or better-optimized kernel) or route requests through a lower-latency region or dedicate GPUs to that workload to avoid noisy neighbors. Also continuous batching and prefix caching reduce cost and sometimes latency variance.
[04:39] Samir: Is model sharding a thing for you?
[04:42] Ethan: For very large models we do sharding at serving layer, but for 13B-level it's single-GPU with optimized kernels. Sharding adds network overhead so generally for 70B+ it matters.
[04:54] Ben: Let's talk about cost comparison — hosted price vs dedicated reserved price.
[04:58] Maya: Hosted is usage-based and good for initial benching. Dedicated has monthly commits and gives you lower per-token costs at scale. We can run pro-forma numbers; I'll pull an example later in the notes.
[05:10] Ethan: Also our Optimize product suggests quant/bsz/batching knobs per workload to cut unit cost without regressing quality.
[05:18] Nina: How do you measure quality regressions? We can't let quantization degrade detection precision.
[05:23] Ethan: We tie quality monitoring to eval suites and real prompt sets — we run baseline prompts and measure task metrics (precision/recall) and if a model/quant change dips below threshold we alert and can auto-fallback to the champion model.
[05:36] Samir: Can that fallback happen within a single request? Like if a quantized run outputs low confidence, does Redwood reroute?
[05:43] Ethan: We can do request-level fallbacks for certain failure modes, or route by policy to a safer model if thresholds breach. It's configurable.
[05:51] Laura: I'd like to understand the bench process — if we share prompt sets do you run them in your hosted infra?
[05:58] Maya: Yes we can run a short hosted bench with your prompts; that's typically 24–72 hours. For private runs we can provide an on-prem harness but that takes more setup.
[06:09] Ben: For our security team, we need SOC2 evidence, KMS setup docs, and an architecture diagram.
[06:16] Maya: We'll share the SOC2 pack and a security checklist after the call.
[06:20] Samir: Great. Can you also include the compatibility matrix exported CSV?
[06:24] Ethan: Yep we'll attach it to the bench sheet.
[06:27] Nina: One more infra question: when you say 'kernel mapping' are you mapping to cuBLAS/cuDNN variants or your own kernels?
[06:36] Ethan: It's a mix. We use vendor libraries where optimal and our own optimized kernels for attention / rotary ops and memory movement — the matrix notes which kernel family produced the bench.
[06:47] Samir: Are there any models you would recommend avoiding for production at this point?
[06:52] Ethan: We flag models with unstable regression history or very high p99 cost. In your case, because you need low p95, we might deprioritize some 13B variants unless they have good kernel support.
[07:04] Maya: To keep this actionable: we've put together a recommended shortlist for your use case — one latency-optimized, one quality-optimized, one cost-optimized. We want you to run the three in a quick bench and pick a champion.
[07:16] Ben: Sounds good. What does the bench deliverable look like?
[07:20] Ethan: Bench sheet with p50/p95/p99, cost per 1k, memory footprints, recommended quant profile, and suggested rollout (canary percentage, fallback model). We'll also provide raw logs if you want to ingest into your observability.
[07:34] Laura: OK. Any legal or procurement blockers we should be aware of?
[07:38] Maya: For pilots under $X we do standard T&Cs; enterprise pilots go through procurement. We can share the SOW template.
[07:46] Samir: One operational question — if we move to dedicated, how do you handle autoscaling?
[07:51] Ethan: Dedicated lets you configure autoscale policies and burst to shared capacity. We surface autoscale events in the console.
[07:59] Nina: For the pilot, what's the minimal data we need to send? We prefer not to send PII.
[08:05] Maya: You can send anonymized prompts or a synthetic dataset representing length/distribution. For quality checks we only need task labels ideally.
[08:14] Ben: Let's go through the shortlist now.
[08:16] Ethan: First model — oxford-13b-lite. Pros: low memory, optimized attention kernels. Cons: slightly lower instruction-following on edge cases. Bench: p95 240ms on A100.
[08:30] Samir: 240ms is borderline.
[08:33] Ethan: Second model — river-7b-instruct: pros very cheap, p95 120ms, but may miss nuanced fraud patterns.
[08:44] Laura: Might be ok as a reranker or quick filter.
[08:47] Ethan: Third — harbor-13b-quant: quality strong, cost mid, p95 310ms as earlier.
[08:55] Ben: Any suggestions to bring harbor p95 down?
[08:58] Ethan: Try a different kernel or increase dedicated GPU reservation to avoid noisy neighbors; also a hybrid routing policy where critical traffic goes to a champion on dedicated.
[09:10] Samir: What about an ensemble approach — small model for fast triage, larger for confirmation?
[09:15] Ethan: Absolutely common pattern. Redwood supports routing policies and post-filtering; you can chain calls or do local logic to call a heavier model if the light model is uncertain.
[09:26] Maya: I'm seeing a question in the chat about model card metadata — we include licenses, training data provenance (where available), and known limitations in the catalog.
[09:38] Nina: That's helpful for compliance.
[09:40] Ben: Ok good. I'm going to hand off to Laura for SSO and network specifics.
[09:45] Laura: For SSO we use Okta SAML, RBAC is important — we need admin roles separated. Can Redwood integrate with SCIM?
[09:54] Maya: Yes we support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning for users and roles.
[09:59] Laura: Great. For network egress, do you provide IP allowlists?
[10:03] Ethan: For hosted we give static egress ranges for allowlist; for private we use your VPC endpoints.
[10:10] Ben: Alright let's move to next steps and assign actions.
[10:14] Maya: Cool, Ethan — could you run a hosted bench with Veridian's prompt set on the three shortlisted models?
[10:20] Ethan: Yep I can do that. I'll need the prompt file and any eval metrics you care about.
[10:25] Samir: We'll share a sanitized prompt set and a small eval harness by EOD tomorrow.
[10:31] Maya: Great. Action items will be: Ethan runs the bench (3-day hosted run), Maya shares SOC2/security pack and SOW template, Veridian to provide anonymized prompt set, and schedule a private-deployment deep dive week of Sep 1.
[10:47] Ben: Can we tentatively book Sep 2 for the SE deep dive?
[10:50] Ethan: Sep 2 works on my side.
[10:53] Maya: I'll send calendar invites after the call.
[10:56] Samir: One more question — do you have any customer case studies in financial services?
[11:01] Maya: Yes, we'll include a short case study about a payments customer that used a two-model routing pattern.
[11:08] Laura: Perfect.
[11:10] Maya: Any other questions?
[11:12] Nina: None from me.
[11:14] Ben: All good. Thanks everyone.
[11:17] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the bench link, security pack, and calendar invites.

End of transcript.
